grammar[0].blocks[2].text: Never at the end, as in English: das Thema, *über das* wir sprechen. For places you can say *wo*: das Café, *wo* wir uns kennengelernt haben.

grammar[0].fact: To found a German *eingetragener Verein* (e.V.) you need seven members, a set of written rules, and a notary. The result is a legal person with tax advantages. Germans have founded them for rabbit breeding, for cleaning a stream, and for preserving the German language.

grammar[1].fact: Every club needs a *Kassenwart*, the treasurer, and two *Kassenprüfer*, who check the treasurer’s accounts once a year and report back. It’s all very serious. When a club closes, it is called *Auflösung*, and there’s a form for that too.

document.intro: A real page from an old book explaining the law on clubs to officials. It is hard, and in old type. But you need only four facts from it. Look at the end of the text, and for the number words.
document.fact: The letters *e.V.* after a club’s name still mean what this page says: *eingetragener Verein*. Germany’s civil code from 1900 set the rule. Seven signatures are still what you need today, and three members may keep a club going.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Join the two sentences with a relative word.
reading.intro: Max now lives in a village near Münster, where the only way to meet people is to join a club. He has joined the Schützenverein, the marksmen, with whom he has shot nothing yet. Tonight is the annual meeting, in the back room of the pub, and he has brought a question.
reading.fact: A *Schützenfest* is still the biggest day of the year in many villages of north-west Germany. The person who shoots the last piece off a wooden bird becomes king for a year, and pays for everyone’s drinks. There are people who deliberately miss, and insurance you can buy in case you don’t.
